set.tovw: 1884 Marshall robbery loot; strangers dug the Dolph stumps 1914 and may have lifted it

tw-mi-bellevue-dolph-stumps.st: The Kalamazoo Gazette (12 Feb 1914) places the digging 'back of the Grohe swamp, which is near the river, and on the Charles Dolph farm'; the two strangers stayed weeks at the Dyer hotel, told Deputy Will Youngs they sought a mineral, and the leader called himself Mosier of Bay City, the name of the c.1884 Marshall robber who fled through Bellevue.
src: Kalamazoo Gazette, 12 Feb 1914, p. 2 (newspapers.com 1144869349; copy Jackson Citizen Patriot same day p. 8, 1162675054)

set.tovw: Third-hand deathbed tale; the local editor called it a fake
set.st: A man dying in Bay City told a nurse that a gambler, dying in California, said he had hidden a large sum in gold on the banks of Mill Creek just above Old Brockway; he had searched many times. The Yale Expositor editor called the story 'a fake'; no sequel. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.

src: Yale Expositor, 14 Oct 1898, p. 4 'Who Will Find It?' (newspapers.com 174792957)

set.tovw: Deathbed words only; no search or find reported
set.st: Cora Miller, daughter of a Hartford farmer, died March 1897; her last words were "Seventeen hundred dollars, dig, dig." The Courier-Northerner's Hartford column (24 Mar 1897) is the only period source: 'Some people suppose that she had money buried'; no search or find was reported. The family farm is on the 1873 and 1895 Van Buren County atlases, and by 1895 Cora held her own forty at its NW corner.

src: Courier-Northerner (Paw Paw), 24 Mar 1897, p. 5, Hartford column (newspapers.com 171911507)
